time: 1 hour later: Day 10, 10:57:12 AM

Out of the story first: yes, there's word on Corvin's statement, and the arbiter reads it to you below.

On the quay, the rain is coming down in sheets. The arbiter looks at the three covered shapes in the skiff, then at you, and nods once. "Pell, the dead to the hall's cold room. Mistress Ashgrove, with me. Your companion too." She's already walking. Kit takes your arm and steers you after her through the rain.

In the Vantry hall's counting-room there's a fire, a clerk with dry cloaks, and a mug of hot cider that tastes like heaven. You give your account in order: the Wick-House at dawn, Ysolde and the staff, Sparrow and the hired boat, the Gullspit light and Brann, the grey cutter, the hooded man called Aldous, the fight, and the lamp that woke. The arbiter listens without interrupting, her stylus moving. When you finish she is quiet for a moment. "The three dead are Heron's Tithe hands, as you say. The cutter is not in the harbour roll, and the master is not a name I know." She lays down the pen. "That is evidence for Dame Crowe's court, and for the Dray reeve. I will hold it under seal."

Then she slides a sheet across the table. "Master Tallowmere signed this at the dawn bell. I read it twice. You asked who the 'H.' was."

You read it. It is in Corvin's neat hand, signed and witnessed. Elowen Ashgrove was his teacher. After she vanished, he was funded and directed for sixteen years by a patron he knew only as "the Grey Factor", who paid for her blessings to be copied into forged tales and chose the houses in the ledger. Sparrow and "Hale", the Thornhallow steward, are the Factor's hands, and the "H." of the note meant Hale's man, Sparrow. The statement doesn't say that Corvin ever saw the Factor's face.

"He asked to see you again," the arbiter adds. "When I mentioned the name Aldous to him this morning, he went white and said nothing more." She sets her hands flat. "You may sleep at the Gull, or stay here. The lamp on the spit has the whole town talking, and I would not have you wandering the quay tonight."

It is nearly eleven. You've no spell slots and one use of Inspiration. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Out of the story first: yes. Corvin dictated his statement, signed it and sealed it before the arbiter and the cellar clerk at nine this morning. It names "H." as Master Hale, and I'll read it to you in a moment.

The arbiter takes in the skiff, the three covered shapes, your soaked cloak and Kit's grey face. Her stylus comes down from behind her ear. "Pell. The dead to the hall's cold room, a physician for the Thistlewood woman, dry cloaks for both. Mistress Ashgrove, you will give me that account, indoors and by a fire. Walk." She doesn't say it unkindly. Through the rain you can see that half the quay has come out to stare at the white light on the spit.

In the hall's counting-room, a stove is roaring. You and Kit sit by it in borrowed blankets while the arbiter writes, and you give the whole account: the hooded man at the beacon, Sparrow, the three hands, the grave, and the name "Aldous". She asks short, hard questions. When you finish, she is quiet for a moment.

"A man in a grey cloak who owns a cutter," she says. "That is a narrow ship-list. I will have the harbour-reeve's book searched for her." Then she slides Corvin's statement across the table. Two close-written pages, signed and sealed, in the neat hand of the cellar clerk.

Corvin names "H." as Master Hale, a go-between who carried the commissions. Behind Hale, he writes, is a lender he has never seen, who buys the debts of minor houses and is repaid in forged pedigrees and deeds. He calls the lender "the Heron." Corvin's man in Saltmarsh was a smiling fellow who called himself Sparrow. He says Elowen was his teacher before he was yours, and he last saw her at Ashby Weir with the child in her arms. He says he never learned how she died. There is no Aldous in it anywhere.

It is past eleven. The squall is rattling the shutters, and you're warm for the first time since morning. You have no spell slots, one use of Bardic Inspiration, and an arbiter who has just handed you a name to chase.

entries.text: notebook: updated Smiling Follower
time: 1 hour 10 minutes later: Day 10, 11:07:12 AM

The arbiter doesn't ask you to repeat yourself. She looks at the three covered shapes in the skiff, then at the white thread of the Gullspit light burning through the rain, and says only, "Indoors. Pell, the dead to the dead-house. Mistress Ashgrove, with me."

The Vantry counting-room has a fire, a bench, and a hot pot of spiced small beer that someone puts into your hands before you've asked. Kit sits against the wall, gripping her cup, still grey from the crossing. You give the account in order: the hired skiff, the Heron's Tithe, the beacon and Brann, the grave, the fight at the door, the lamp. You give the names too, Sparrow and the hooded man called Aldous. The arbiter writes everything down and asks short, exact questions. The Heron's Tithe is a known vessel, she says, and the harbourmaster will want a word with whoever owns her.

Then she answers your other question. Corvin dictated his statement to the Vantry clerk last night. It runs to six close-written pages, signed in the arbiter's own presence this morning. She hands it over, and you read it by the fire.

It says that "H." is Sparrow, whose true name is Harrow, a hand of the man called Aldous. Aldous, Corvin writes, is a former priest of the Lantern-Bearer who has hunted the road-priest Elowen's lamp-staff and her daughter for sixteen years. Master Hale of Thornhallow was Aldous's hired hand, planted at Lord Edric's table to see what the Verrel charter would bring. According to the statement, Aldous paid for the forgeries sold to Verrel, Thistlewood and Dray as a means of finding a road to the staff, and to you. Corvin claims he was afraid. The statement does not say whether he believed any of it himself, and you remember how well he can write a plausible page.

The arbiter folds her hands. "The harbourmaster has set a watch on the east quay for the Tithe's return. Sir Corwen sends word that the keep's door is open to you. And the Vantry elder asks, humbly, whether you'll accept a hot bath." Her mouth twitches. "I think you should."

It's past eleven, you have no spell slots, and a night's sleep would be welcome. Aldous and Harrow know where your reliquary is. What does Wren do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Master Hale
time: 1 hour 10 minutes later: Day 10, 11:07:12 AM

Out of the story first, on your question: yes. Corvin signed his statement at dawn, and it names "H." You'll hear it read in a moment.

The arbiter's mouth tightens as she looks at the three covered shapes in the skiff. She says nothing for the space of a breath. Then she nods. "Pell, take the dead to the dead-house and have a clerk list their marks. Bring the mistress and her companion to the hall, and bring a fire." She turns and walks, and you follow, wringing out your cloak.

In the Vantry hall's side-room a fire is lit, hot spiced cider appears, and Kit is wrapped in a Vantry blanket and sits with her boots steaming. The account takes a little over an hour. You give it plainly: the Wick-House, Sparrow, the Heron's Tithe, the Gullspit light, Brann, the grey-cloaked man called Aldous, three hands dead at the north door. The arbiter writes steadily and doesn't interrupt. When you finish, she lays down her stylus and draws a folded sheet from her sleeve.

"Master Tallowmere's statement," she says. "Signed at the dawn bell. He dictated it to my clerk without once raising his voice." She reads out the parts that matter. Elowen Ashgrove was his teacher; he last saw her alive at Ashby Weir; he searched and found the coffer and the Wick-House, but never the Gullspit light. And the man he called "H." is Master Hale, steward of Thornhallow, in the pay of a sea-road man who calls himself Aldous. Hale bought Corvin's forged tales to hook minor houses and trace Elowen's daughter. "He writes," she says, "that he took the money because it was good, and kept the trail because he was ashamed. I make no judgment on that."

So Hale, held at Thornhallow for Dame Crowe, was only one of Aldous's hands. Sparrow and the cutter are loose, and Aldous is out on the grey water.

The arbiter folds the sheet. "I'll send this to Dame Crowe's court with a rider today, with a note that the hall holds three dead of the Heron's Tithe. You will want to be in Marrowford at month's end." She looks at you for a moment, not unkindly. "And you've had no sleep to speak of, mistress. Eat. Rest. You've the look of a lamp that's burned its oil."

It is past eleven. You've one hit die per level unspent, no spell slots, and one use of Bardic Inspiration left. Kit is at 15 of 20. A short rest would give you back some, and the Salt Gull has beds. The Gullspit light still burns on the horizon, and the grey cutter may return. What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 12 ~12:33 AM: shot Wren twice through the shutter (10 damage), then, bleeding with 1 HP left, dropped his hand crossbow and surrendered. Alive in Wren's custody at the Rushlight House yard. A hired scout (Scout stat block), hooded, brown cloak, pale horse on the dike. Name and master not yet learned.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow's Watcher

You drop below the sill and speak the Lantern-Bearer's word to yourself. The charm knits your ribs, and you heal 4 (11 of 17), with one slot left. Then you rise and snap your mockery through the gap: "You're bleeding, friend, and the horse is farther than the hook!" The insult lands. His save is an 8, he takes 3, and he's down to a single hit point. He sways, and the cold violet light shows every drop of blood on his sleeve.

You call the rest across the yard, and it carries. "Surrender now, and you'll leave with a bandage and your life. Run, and Kit shoots you in the back." Behind him you hear the byre door creak and the ferry-hook scrape the stones as Tamsin steps out of the shadows.

He looks at the dike, then at Kit's crossbow and the hook, and at what is left of his sleeve. Then he opens his hand and lets the hand crossbow fall onto the shingle. He puts both hands out to his sides, slowly. The hood stays up, and his voice is dry and shaky from under it. "Gently, mistress. I'm only the eyes." Your concentration lets the spell lapse and the light fades, leaving him a grey shape in the dark. The fight is over after three rounds. You earn 100 XP, so you're at 475 of 900.

He's alive, hurt and unarmed, standing ten paces from the shutter in the yard. Kit has the crossbow trained on him, and Tamsin is closing from the ferry shed. Annis calls quietly from behind the hearth, "Is it done?"

It is half past midnight. You've 11 of 17 hit points, one 1st-level slot, and two Bardic Inspirations. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 12 ~12:33 AM: fought at Reedlow (Scout stat block, hand crossbow); brought to 4 HP by Kit's crossbow and surrendered, dropping his weapon. Prisoner of Wren and Kit. Not Sparrow himself (younger, hooded, shorter). Awaiting questioning.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow's Watcher

You duck below the sill and say the Lantern-Bearer's word to your own ribs. The stinging in your side eases, and you heal 7 to 14 of 17, with one slot left. Then you pop up at the gap and call it across the yard, loud enough for the whole village: "Surrender now, and you'll leave with a bandage and your life. Run, and Kit shoots you in the back."

Your insult about the horse lands on stone. His Wisdom save is a 15 and he shrugs it off. But the rest of it lands. He stands in the violet light with blood running down his sleeve, looks at the dike where his horse is a long way off, and hears Kit's crossbow ratchet in the dark behind him. Tamsin steps out of the ferry-shed shadow with the hook up and says nothing. It's quite enough.

The little crossbow clatters onto the shingle. He drops to one knee with both hands raised. "All right," he says, hoarse, young, with the accent of the lower river. "All right, mistress. I yield."

You release Faerie Fire, and the cold light fades from him. The fight is over in eighteen seconds. You get 100 XP for the scout, so you have 475 of 900.

He is a lean, hooded man in his twenties. He's not Sparrow, who is older and smiles more. He's bleeding from the shoulder and ribs and he is shaking, partly from pain and partly from fear. Kit comes out of the byre with her sword drawn and her shield up and stands over him without a word. It's half past midnight, and Annis is calling quietly from within: "Is it done?"

He is your prisoner. What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.
